As the M6 Mac mini and its more powerful M5 Pro variant officially go on sale, Apple has quietly removed one of the most attractive selling points of this machine. Although the two new Mac minis look identical to the previous generation on the outside, Apple has eliminated a hidden feature that was present on the last-generation Mac mini — a feature that made it an incredibly good-value machine.

When the M4 Mac mini first launched, its value for money was off the charts. In addition to featuring Apple's own M4 SoC, it came standard with 16GB of unified memory, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, two front-facing USB 3 ports, HDMI and Ethernet. Priced at US$599, with a student price as low as US$499, the M4 Mac mini was not only the most versatile Mac across Apple's entire product lineup, but also offered the best overall performance.

影片：Apple 殺死咗 Mac mini 最佳嘅隱藏功能 :(

However, Apple's smallest Mac had another trump card that made it even more of a bargain: a built-in upgradeable storage slot. Users only had to pry off the back panel and unscrew a few screws to access a removable NAND module, which could easily be swapped out for a third-party SSD, supporting up to 2TB.

This design brought many benefits. Users could not only upgrade the SSD or easily deal with drive failures, but also save a considerable amount of money — no need to opt for Apple's custom upgrade options, just buy a much cheaper third-party SSD and you're set.

At the time, Apple priced the 2TB upgrade at US$800, so simply ticking that option would turn this "budget" computer into a US$1,400 machine. By upgrading with a third-party SSD after purchase, users could save nearly US$500.

As someone who enjoys building PCs myself, I was naturally thrilled, and I even produced a full video tutorial walking through step by step how to upgrade the factory SSD with a third-party drive. The video received an enthusiastic response, accumulating 500,000 views.

影片：點樣升級 M4 Mac mini 嘅 SSD

Good times did not last.

With this generation of Mac mini, Apple has soldered the SSD directly onto the motherboard, completely eliminating the possibility for users to upgrade with a third-party NAND module after purchase.

The Mac mini has gone from being the undisputed best-value Mac to a product that is noticeably much more expensive — not only has the base model jumped from US$600 to US$900, but the 2TB upgrade has also increased from US$800 to US$1,000.

At current pricing, if you want an M6 Mac mini with 2TB of SSD, you inevitably have to pay Apple US$1,900. Compared to the previous-generation M4 Mac mini, which at the time cost around US$920 to get to 2TB when factoring in the US$320 post-purchase upgrade. Of course, prices fluctuate over time and cannot be directly compared (you know how it is with Apple), but the price here is a full US$1,000 more. Beyond Apple raising prices aggressively, the bigger reason is that they have outright taken away users' right to upgrade the machine themselves.

I can roughly guess why Apple raised the price of the base Mac mini by US$300, and the surge in SSD prices is something I can also understand. Driven by factors such as AI, the costs of components, SSDs and memory have all risen significantly. But none of this explains why Apple chose to solder the SSD onto the motherboard instead of retaining the previous user-replaceable design.

How did Apple arrive at the decision to revert to soldering the SSD? We can speculate, but we will never know the real answer. What is certain is that the price of these machines has risen dramatically — saying "dramatically" might even be an understatement. Comparing the M4 Mac mini from back then, configured with a 2TB post-purchase upgrade, to the M6 Mac mini today, configured with a 2TB custom upgrade, the price has increased by roughly 106%.

9to5Mac 觀點

It's not that easy to find a base M4 Mac mini at a reasonable price on the second-hand market right now, but if you do manage to find one, it remains an exceptional machine in terms of performance, features and upgradeable SSD.

The only good news is that all Mac mini models come with Thunderbolt connectivity, allowing users to easily add high-speed external storage via USB or Thunderbolt SSDs. Personally, I'm particularly fond of the Samsung T9, which is a relatively affordable storage expansion solution.

What do you think led Apple to abandon the user-replaceable SSD design on the Mac mini? Any unique insights? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
